events.title: Huns raid Armenia, Cappadocia and Syria through the Caucasus
events.summary: In 395, while the eastern army was still in Italy after the Frigidus, Hunnic horsemen crossed the Caucasus by the Caspian Gates and ravaged Armenia, Cappadocia, Cilicia and Syria, threatening Antioch and Edessa. Jerome, at Bethlehem, describes the panic and the hasty repair of Jerusalem's walls. The raiders withdrew with captives; the eunuch Eutropius claimed a victory over them in 398.

events.title: Augustine writes the Confessions
events.summary: Newly bishop of Hippo, Augustine wrote the thirteen books of the Confessions between about 397 and 401: a prayer addressed to God recounting his youth at Thagaste and Carthage, his Manichaean years, his career as rhetor in Rome and Milan and his conversion in a Milanese garden in 386. It created the genre of introspective autobiography.

events.title: Revolt of Tribigild in Phrygia
events.summary: Tribigild, commander of Gothic federates settled in Phrygia, revolted in spring 399 after being snubbed by Eutropius and plundered Phrygia, Pisidia and Pamphylia. The general Leo was defeated and Gainas, sent against him, colluded with the rebels and demanded the fall of Eutropius, triggering the Gothic crisis of 399-400 in Constantinople.

events.title: Destruction of the Marneion at Gaza
events.summary: With an imperial order said to have been obtained from Empress Eudoxia at the birth of Theodosius II, Bishop Porphyry of Gaza had the city's great temple of Marnas burned in 402 and a cruciform church, the Eudoxiana, built on its site, using its marble paving for a pathway so that pagans would tread on it.
events.debate: The Life of Porphyry attributed to Mark the Deacon may be a sixth-century composition; its details are doubtful, though the destruction of the Marneion is broadly accepted.

events.title: Synod of the Oak
events.summary: In summer 403 Theophilus of Alexandria and 36 mostly Egyptian bishops met at the imperial estate called 'the Oak' near Chalcedon and deposed John Chrysostom on 29 charges, with the backing of Empress Eudoxia. John was exiled, recalled within days after riots and a portent in the palace, and finally exiled for good in 404.

sources.w: Dialogue on the Life of John Chrysostom

events.title: Mesrop Mashtots creates the Armenian alphabet
events.summary: Around 405, with the support of Catholicos Sahak and King Vramshapuh, the cleric Mesrop Mashtots devised a 36-letter alphabet for Armenian, followed by alphabets for Georgian and Caucasian Albanian according to his biographer Koriwn. The first texts were translations of Proverbs and the Bible, inaugurating Armenian literature.

events.title: Jerome completes his translation of the Old Testament from Hebrew
events.summary: Working at Bethlehem from about 390, Jerome translated the Hebrew Bible directly into Latin rather than from the Greek Septuagint, completing it around 405. Augustine objected that it would separate the Latin church from the Greek; the translation became the core of the Vulgate, the Bible of the Latin West until modern times.

events.title: Gerontius proclaims Maximus in Spain
events.summary: Constantine III's general Gerontius rebelled in Spain in 409 and proclaimed his own dependant Maximus emperor, probably at Tarraco, apparently letting the Vandals, Alans and Suebi into the peninsula. He killed Constantine's son Constans at Vienne and besieged Arles in 411, but his troops deserted when Honorius's general Constantius arrived; Gerontius killed his wife and himself in his burning house.

events.title: Synod of Seleucia-Ctesiphon
events.summary: Under the tolerant Yazdegerd I, the Roman envoy Marutha of Maypherqat and the catholicos Isaac convened a synod of the Persian church in 410 that adopted the Nicene creed and canons and organised the church under the bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon. The King of Kings allowed it to meet; it laid the foundation of the Church of the East.

events.title: Honoratus founds the monastery of Lérins
events.summary: Around 410 the aristocrat Honoratus settled on the island of Lerina off Cannes and founded a monastery that became the training ground of the Gallic episcopate: Hilary of Arles, Eucherius of Lyon, Lupus of Troyes, Faustus of Riez and later Caesarius of Arles all passed through it. It linked monasticism to the Gallo-Roman aristocracy.

events.title: Usurpation of Jovinus at Mainz
events.summary: A Gallo-Roman noble, Jovinus, was proclaimed emperor at Mainz in 411 with the support of the Burgundian king Gundahar and the Alan king Goar. Athaulf's Goths at first joined him but changed sides; Athaulf killed Jovinus's brother Sebastianus, and Jovinus, besieged at Valence in 413, was handed over and executed at Narbonne by the prefect Dardanus.

events.title: Conference of Carthage
events.summary: From 1 to 8 June 411 the imperial tribune Marcellus presided over a debate between 286 Catholic and 279 Donatist bishops in the Baths of Gargilius at Carthage. Augustine led the Catholic case. Marcellus ruled for the Catholics; the edict of 412 outlawed Donatism, confiscating its churches and fining its adherents. The stenographic minutes partly survive.

events.title: Revolt of Heraclianus
events.summary: Heraclianus, comes Africae, who had personally killed Stilicho in 408 and kept Africa loyal against Attalus, rebelled in 413, held back the grain fleet and sailed for Italy with an armada Orosius absurdly numbers at 3,700 ships. Defeated after landing near Rome, he fled back to Carthage, where he was executed. His property went to Constantius.

events.title: Burgundians settled on the left bank of the Rhine
events.summary: Prosper records that in 413 the Burgundians obtained the part of Gaul adjoining the Rhine, apparently as federates of Jovinus confirmed by Honorius's government. Later legend placed their capital at Worms under King Gundahar (Gunther of the Nibelungenlied). Aetius and his Huns destroyed this kingdom in 436.
events.debate: Worms as the Burgundian centre rests on the Nibelung tradition; the location is uncertain.

events.title: Murder of Athaulf at Barcelona
events.summary: Athaulf, who had married Galla Placidia and lost their infant son Theodosius, was stabbed in a stable at Barcelona in August or September 415 by a retainer avenging his former master Sarus. His successor Sigeric killed Athaulf's children by an earlier marriage and made Placidia walk before his horse with other captives, but was murdered after seven days; Wallia succeeded.

events.title: Synod of Diospolis acquits Pelagius
events.summary: In December 415 fourteen Palestinian bishops at Diospolis (Lydda) heard charges brought by two exiled Gallic bishops and acquitted Pelagius after he disowned some of his disciple Caelestius's propositions. Augustine responded with De gestis Pelagii, and the African councils of 416-418 secured papal and imperial condemnation.

events.title: Rutilius Namatianus's De reditu suo
events.summary: In autumn 417 the Gallic pagan aristocrat Rutilius Namatianus, former urban prefect, sailed from Rome to his ravaged estates in Gaul and described the voyage in elegiacs. His hymn to Rome contains the line 'you made one fatherland of diverse peoples', while he attacks Jews, monks and Stilicho, whom he accuses of burning the Sibylline Books.

events.title: John Cassian at Marseille: the Institutes and Conferences
events.summary: John Cassian, who had lived among the monks of Egypt, founded two monasteries at Marseille around 415 and wrote the Institutes (c. 420) and Conferences (c. 426-429), transmitting Egyptian desert spirituality to the Latin West. His semi-Pelagian views on grace drew attacks from Prosper of Aquitaine, but Benedict prescribed his works for monastic reading.

events.title: The Law of Citations
events.summary: A constitution issued at Ravenna on 7 November 426 in the name of the child Valentinian III restricted courts to the writings of five jurists, Papinian, Paul, Ulpian, Modestinus and Gaius. Where they disagreed the majority prevailed, and on a tie Papinian's view decided. It sought certainty in a legal system swamped by conflicting authorities.

events.title: End of the Arsacid kingdom of Armenia
events.summary: At the request of Armenian nobles hostile to King Artashir IV, Bahram V deposed him in 428, ending the Arsacid dynasty that had ruled Armenia since the first century AD. Persarmenia became a province under a Persian marzban, while the Roman sector had already been absorbed into the empire.

events.title: End of the Jewish patriarchate
events.summary: The Jewish patriarch Gamaliel VI was stripped of his honorary prefecture in 415 for building synagogues and owning Christian slaves. By 429 a law refers to the time 'after the passing of the patriarchs' and diverts to the imperial treasury the annual dues Jews had paid to the patriarchate. The office of the Nasi, recognised by Rome since the third century, lapsed.

events.title: Theodosius II orders a codification of imperial laws
events.summary: On 26 March 429 Theodosius II ordered a commission to collect all general constitutions issued since Constantine and to prepare a second, more ambitious code combining laws with juristic writings. The second plan was abandoned; a new commission of sixteen under Antiochus, appointed in 435, completed the Codex Theodosianus in 437.

events.title: The so-called Mausoleum of Galla Placidia
events.summary: A small cruciform chapel attached to Galla Placidia's church of Santa Croce in Ravenna, built c. 425-450, with the most complete early Christian mosaic interior to survive: a starry vault, the Good Shepherd, and St Lawrence with his gridiron. Placidia died in Rome in 450 and was probably buried there, not in this building.

events.title: Palladius sent to the Irish; the mission of Patrick
events.summary: Prosper records that in 431 Pope Celestine ordained Palladius 'first bishop to the Irish believing in Christ'. The more famous mission of Patrick, a Romano-British decurion's son once enslaved in Ireland, is traditionally dated to 432; his own Confessio and Letter to Coroticus are the only texts surviving from fifth-century Britain or Ireland written by a named individual.
events.debate: Patrick's dates are uncertain; some place his mission later in the fifth century.

events.title: Santa Maria Maggiore built by Sixtus III
events.summary: Soon after the Council of Ephesus proclaimed Mary Theotokos, Pope Sixtus III (432-440) built the great basilica on the Esquiline dedicated to the Virgin, whose triumphal arch inscription reads 'Xystus episcopus plebi Dei'. Its nave mosaics of Old Testament scenes are the largest surviving cycle of fifth-century Roman mosaic.

events.title: The Bacaudae of Tibatto
events.summary: The Gallic Chronicle of 452 says that in 435 'farther Gaul followed Tibatto, the leader of the rebellion, and seceded from Roman society; from this beginning almost all the servile population of Gaul conspired in Bacaudae'. Aetius's general Litorius crushed the revolt by 437. The nature of the Bacaudae, peasant rebels or local self-defence, remains debated.

events.title: The Suebi take Mérida
events.summary: King Rechila of the Suebi took Emerita Augusta, capital of the diocese of the Spains, in 439 and Hispalis in 441, making the Suebi masters of Lusitania, Baetica and Carthaginiensis. Hydatius, bishop in Gallaecia, records the conquest from the Roman provincials' point of view.

events.title: Brief Roman-Persian war of 440
events.summary: Yazdegerd II attacked Roman territory around 440, perhaps over Roman fortifications and Christian refugees, while Roman forces were committed against the Vandals. The magister militum per Orientem Anatolius made a quick peace in which both sides agreed not to build new forts near the border, a clause later invoked against Anastasius's Dara.

events.title: Salvian's On the Government of God
events.summary: The Marseille priest Salvian argued in De gubernatione Dei (c. 440) that the barbarian conquests were God's just punishment of Roman vice, contrasting chaste Goths and Vandals with corrupt Romans, and that oppressed provincials fled to the Bacaudae or the barbarians to escape tax collectors. It is a central text for the social history of the western collapse.

events.title: Huns sack Viminacium, Margus, Singidunum and Sirmium
events.summary: Accusing the bishop of Margus of robbing Hunnic royal tombs, Attila and Bleda crossed the Danube in 441 while Roman forces were in Sicily for the Vandal expedition. The bishop betrayed Margus to save himself; Viminacium, Singidunum and Sirmium fell. Excavated Viminacium shows abandonment after this date.

events.title: Treaty of 442 with Gaiseric
events.summary: After the aborted eastern expedition, Valentinian III recognised Gaiseric's possession of Proconsularis, Byzacena and eastern Numidia, the richest provinces of the West, in exchange for the return of the Mauretanias and western Numidia. Gaiseric's son Huneric, a hostage in Italy, was betrothed to Valentinian's daughter Eudocia, and Huneric's Visigothic wife was sent home mutilated.

events.title: Aetius settles Alans at Valence and Orléans
events.summary: The Gallic Chronicle records that Aetius gave deserted lands around Valence to Alans under Sambida (440) and settled the Alans of King Goar in farther Gaul (442), where they expelled the landowners by force. These Alans, based on Orléans, fought for Aetius at the Catalaunian Plains in 451.

events.title: Burgundians settled in Sapaudia
events.summary: The surviving Burgundians, broken by the Huns in 436, were settled by Aetius in 443 in Sapaudia, the region around Lake Geneva, 'to be divided with the natives', according to the Gallic Chronicle. From this base they expanded down the Rhône to create the kingdom of Gundioc, Chilperic and Gundobad centred on Lyon and Geneva.

events.title: Attila murders Bleda
events.summary: Around 445 Attila killed his elder brother and co-ruler Bleda and became sole king of the Huns. Bleda's widow continued to hold a village, where Priscus's embassy was entertained in 449, and Bleda's Moorish jester Zercon was passed to Aetius.

events.title: Valentinian III's law on papal authority
events.summary: On 8 July 445, at Pope Leo I's request, Valentinian III issued a constitution (Novel 17) declaring that the primacy of the apostolic see was confirmed by Peter's merit, Rome's dignity and a holy synod, and ordering provincial governors to compel bishops to attend the pope's tribunal. It was aimed at Hilary of Arles and gave imperial sanction to papal jurisdiction over the western church.

events.title: The Tome of Leo
events.summary: On 13 June 449 Pope Leo I sent Patriarch Flavian of Constantinople a dogmatic letter condemning Eutyches and defining Christ as one person in two natures, each performing what is proper to it. Suppressed at Ephesus II, it was acclaimed at Chalcedon with the cry 'Peter has spoken through Leo' and became the touchstone of Chalcedonian orthodoxy and the main target of its opponents.

events.title: Marcian stops the tribute to Attila
events.summary: Marcian, on his accession in August 450, executed the eunuch Chrysaphius and announced that he would no longer pay Attila the 2,100 lb of gold a year agreed in 447, offering gifts only for peace and war for aggression. Attila, drawn to the West by the Honoria affair, never turned on the East, where Marcian's refusal and the Hunnic collapse left a full treasury.

events.title: Assassination of Thorismund
events.summary: Thorismund, who had succeeded his father Theodoric I on the Catalaunian battlefield, was murdered in 453 at Toulouse by his brothers Theodoric II and Frederic, reputedly for his anti-Roman policy. Theodoric II became a close ally of Aetius's successors and of the emperor Avitus.

events.title: The Codex Encyclius
events.summary: Leo I, unsure whether to uphold Chalcedon, wrote in 457-458 to the metropolitans and leading holy men of the empire asking their opinion on the council and on Timothy Aelurus. The replies, collected as the Codex Encyclius, overwhelmingly supported Chalcedon, and Timothy was exiled to Gangra and then Cherson in 460.

events.title: Murder of Patriarch Proterius of Alexandria
events.summary: When news of Marcian's death reached Alexandria in early 457, anti-Chalcedonians consecrated Timothy Aelurus ('the Cat') patriarch, and on Holy Thursday, 28 March 457, a mob killed the Chalcedonian patriarch Proterius in the baptistery, dragged his body through the city and burned it. It marked Egypt's lasting rejection of Chalcedon.

events.title: The Orthodox (Neonian) Baptistery of Ravenna
events.summary: The octagonal baptistery beside Ravenna's cathedral, begun under Bishop Ursus around 400, was given its mosaic dome under Bishop Neon c. 450-460: the baptism of Christ, with a personified river Jordan, surrounded by the twelve apostles. It is the best-preserved baptistery of the fifth century.

events.title: Earthquake at Antioch
events.summary: On 13-14 September 458 an earthquake destroyed much of the New City on the Orontes island at Antioch, including part of the palace and colonnades. Evagrius, citing earlier chroniclers, lists the buildings lost. It was the first of a series of catastrophes, culminating in 526 and 528, that ended Antioch's classical prosperity.

events.title: Death of Simeon the Stylite
events.summary: Simeon, who had lived on top of a column near Telanissos in northern Syria since about 423, raising it in stages to some 18 m, died on 2 September 459. His body was taken to Antioch under military guard. Pilgrims from as far as Gaul and Britain had visited him; the vast cruciform pilgrimage church of Qal'at Sim'an was built round his column c. 476-490.

events.title: Death of Aegidius
events.summary: Aegidius, Majorian's magister militum in Gaul who refused to recognise Ricimer's emperors and ruled an independent command in the north, died in 465, by poison or ambush according to Hydatius. He had sent envoys to the Vandals proposing an alliance. His son Syagrius inherited his power at Soissons.

events.title: Great fire of Constantinople
events.summary: A fire that started in the dockside quarter on the Golden Horn on 2 September 465 burned for days and destroyed, according to Evagrius, eight of the city's fourteen regions, including the area from the Neorion to the Forum of Constantine. Leo I moved to the palace of St Mamas for six months.

events.title: Tarasis the Isaurian becomes Zeno and marries Ariadne
events.summary: The Isaurian chieftain Tarasis son of Kodisa, from Rousoumblada, won Leo I's favour in 466 by producing letters proving that Aspar's son Ardabur was intriguing with Persia. He took the Greek name Zeno, married Leo's daughter Ariadne and became magister militum, creating an Isaurian counterweight to Aspar's Gothic following.

events.title: Death of Dengizich
events.summary: Attila's son Dengizich, who had crossed the frozen Danube against the empire, was defeated and killed in 469 by the magister militum per Thracias Anagast. His head was brought to Constantinople, paraded through the streets and fixed on a pole at the Xylokirkos for days. It marks the end of Hunnic power in the Balkans.

events.title: Euric defeats Anthemius's son near Arles
events.summary: Anthemius sent his son Anthemiolus with the generals Thorisarius, Everdingus and Hermianus to stop Euric's expansion; they were defeated and killed by the Visigoths east of the Rhône near Arles in 471. It was the last campaign of an imperial army in Gaul and left the Auvergne isolated.

battle.significance: Last imperial army in Gaul destroyed.

events.title: Euric conquers Tarraconensis
events.summary: In 472-473 Euric's count Gauterit took Pamplona, Zaragoza and the neighbouring cities, while Heldefred with Vincentius besieged Tarragona and took the coastal cities of Tarraconensis, the last Roman province in Spain. Visigothic rule now covered most of the peninsula outside Suebic Gallaecia.

events.title: Leo I's treaty with Theodoric Strabo
events.summary: After Strabo's Thracian Goths rebelled following Aspar's murder, Leo I agreed in 473 to pay them 2,000 lb of gold a year, to make Strabo magister militum praesentalis and to recognise him as sole king of the Goths, provided he served the emperor against all enemies except the Vandals.

events.title: Julius Nepos cedes the Auvergne to Euric
events.summary: After four years of resistance led by Sidonius Apollinaris and Ecdicius, Nepos's envoys, among them Epiphanius of Pavia, ceded the Auvergne to Euric in 475 in exchange for Provence. Sidonius wrote bitterly that 'our servitude has been made the price of others' security'. He was imprisoned by the Goths before being restored to his see.

events.title: The Encyclical of Basiliscus
events.summary: Basiliscus issued an encyclical in 475 anathematising the Tome of Leo and Chalcedon and recalled Timothy Aelurus. Constantinople rose against it; the stylite Daniel came down from his column for the only time to lead the protest. Basiliscus retracted with an Antencyclical in 476, too late to save his throne from Zeno.
